description: We are Nyms Orbit, a team passionate about space exploration and innovative technology. Led by a Computer Science student with experience in software and web development, we're building an interactive Martian map using NASA data to support exploration and mission planning. We're looking for creative teammates skilled in UI/UX, GIS, 3D visualization, data science, and planetary science. Let's explore Mars together!
summary:
Jezero Crater Explorer is an interactive Martian map that helps astronauts plan safer and more efficient exploration routes across Jezero Crater.

Our application combines NASA satellite imagery, thermal imagery, and elevation data to visualize the Martian surface, identify steep terrain, and calculate routes based on slope limits, walking speed, and available mission time.

Users can explore the terrain, compare alternative routes, and access information about elevation, distance, cumulative ascent, and estimated travel time.

Our project addresses the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge by demonstrating how real planetary data can support astronaut safety, mission planning, and scientific exploration on Mars, particularly in areas that may contain evidence of ancient water and past habitability.
details:
Project Overview

Jezero Crater Explorer is an interactive web application designed to help astronauts explore the Martian surface and plan safer routes using real planetary data.

Our project focuses on a simulated scientific mission from Octavia E. Butler Landing to Belva Crater, where exposed geological layers could help scientists investigate the history of water and past habitability on Mars.

How It Works

The application combines three major planetary datasets:

  • THEMIS Daytime Infrared imagery from Mars Odyssey for regional surface visualization.
  • HiRISE imagery from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter for detailed surface observation.
  • USGS CTX Digital Elevation Model (DEM), with a resolution of 20 meters per pixel, for elevation and terrain slope analysis.

We processed the elevation data using Python, NumPy, and Rasterio and calculated terrain slopes using Horn's method.

We implemented an A* pathfinding algorithm that considers distance, terrain slope, and user-defined safety limits when calculating routes.

Users can customize their mission by adjusting the maximum acceptable slope, walking speed, and available mission time.

The application provides:

  • Interactive planetary map layers.
  • Real-time elevation and slope information.
  • Hazardous terrain visualization.
  • Automatic route calculation.
  • Estimated round-trip travel time.
  • Total distance and cumulative ascent.
  • Mission time budget warnings.

Technology Stack

  • React and JavaScript
  • Vite
  • Mapbox GL JS
  • Python
  • NumPy, Rasterio, and Pillow
  • A* pathfinding algorithm
  • NASA and USGS planetary datasets

Innovation and Creativity

Instead of simply displaying satellite imagery, we transformed scientific planetary data into an interactive mission-planning tool.

Our application demonstrates why the shortest route is not necessarily the safest route. Users can compare different terrain restrictions and understand how safety considerations affect distance, climbing effort, and mission duration.

Intended Impact

Our goal is to demonstrate how accessible planetary data and intelligent route-planning algorithms can support future human exploration of Mars.

The application also serves as an educational tool, helping students, researchers, and space enthusiasts understand the challenges astronauts may face when navigating unfamiliar planetary environments.

This project is a proof of concept rather than an operational astronaut navigation system.
